name: Shannon Foynes
title: Shannon Estuary Ship Thickness Measurement | Foynes UTM
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement at Foynes, Limerick and the Shannon Estuary: bulk carrier and tanker gauging, hold and tank structure, piping and CAP work.
h1: Ultrasonic Hull Gauging on the Shannon Estuary at Foynes and Limerick
intro: The Shannon Estuary is the longest stretch of deep, sheltered water on Ireland's west coast, and Foynes, Limerick and the private jetties of the estuary's industrial sites take bulk carriers, tankers and project cargo through the year. Ships come here to discharge feed, grain, fertiliser, coal, petroleum coke and bauxite, and many are gauged during that discharge for a survey that falls due soon afterwards. Our technicians travel from India to the estuary and board at the berth or at anchor.

highlights.p: Feed, grain, fertiliser and coal ships spend several days at the Foynes quays, which suits hold and hopper tank gauging in stages as each space is cleared. A ship due a renewal survey can have its steel picture fixed before the next yard call.

highlights.h: Private jetties with their own rules
highlights.p: The alumina refinery at Aughinish and the estuary's power stations run their own jetties under terminal permits. Gauging there is fitted to the cargo schedule and arranged through the ship's agent with the terminal's agreement.

Scattery Roads and the estuary's other anchorages let a ship waiting for a berth be gauged on the hook, tide and weather permitting. Tanks cleared ahead of the next cargo can be measured while the ship waits its turn.

port.h: The Shannon Estuary: Ireland's deep-water bulk gateway on the Atlantic
p: The Shannon Estuary opens to the Atlantic between Loop Head and Kerry Head and runs inland to Limerick, with deep water for most of its length. Shannon Foynes Port Company is the harbour authority for the whole estuary, and pilotage is a normal part of every large ship's passage. Foynes sits on the south shore, on the lee side of Foynes Island, where the main commercial quays face a channel with strong tidal streams. Further down the estuary the Tarbert and Moneypoint power stations and the Aughinish refinery each have their own jetty, and Limerick's older docks lie at the head of navigation.

Traffic is dominated by dry and liquid bulk. Foynes handles animal feed ingredients, grain, fertiliser, coal, petroleum coke, ores and scrap, with petroleum products and other liquids discharged at dedicated berths. The refinery at Aughinish takes in bauxite and chemicals by sea and ships alumina out, while the power stations have historically received their fuel by bulk carrier and tanker. Handysize and Supramax bulk carriers are the commonest callers, with product tankers, coasters and the occasional large bulker lightening or discharging in several stages. Project cargo, including wind-energy components, is a growing part of the mix.

Seasonality follows agriculture and energy demand. Feed and fertiliser imports rise through the spring and autumn, grain cargoes cluster after harvest, and fuel deliveries respond to power-station requirements. West-coast weather is the main planning variable: swell at the estuary mouth can delay a pilot boarding, and southwesterly gales affect launch work at the outer anchorages far more than at the sheltered inner berths. Ships frequently wait at anchor for a berth, so the same visit often offers both an anchorage window and a berth window for different parts of a gauging scope.

facilities.h: Where ships are gauged on the Shannon Estuary
p: There is no drydock on the estuary, so a ship that needs a docking leaves for a yard on another coast. What the estuary offers instead is long, calm berth time. At the Foynes quays a bulk carrier is typically discharged over several days, and that gives a gauging team time to work through the topside, hopper and double-bottom ballast tanks while discharge continues, then enter the cargo holds one by one as the grabs finish. Deck, hatch cover and coaming gauging can proceed alongside the cargo work wherever the stevedores have cleared the area.

At the private jetties the rules change from berth to berth. Tanker and chemical calls are bound by gas-free requirements, and work in tanks is restricted until the master and the terminal accept the certificate. Dry bulk jetties at the power stations and the refinery work to the discharge rate of the cargo, so a short stay favours a focused scope of piping, deck and a few prepared tanks. Anchorage work depends on the launch and the sea state, and is kept for ships that have already cleaned and ventilated the spaces concerned.
list: Foynes deep-water quays — hold, hopper and topside tank gauging on bulk carriers during multi-day discharge, with deck and hatch coamings gauged between grab cycles.
Foynes Island liquid bulk berths — piping, deck and released-tank gauging on product tankers, within the terminal's permit and gas-free rules.
Aughinish refinery jetty — hull and deck gauging on bauxite and chemical carriers during the refinery's discharge programme.
Power-station jetties at Tarbert and Moneypoint — focused deck, piping and prepared-tank gauging on fuel-supply ships alongside.
Limerick docks — general cargo and bulk calls at the head of the estuary, where smaller ships can lie for a few days.
Scattery Roads and estuary anchorages — launch-borne gauging of cleaned tanks on ships waiting for a berth.

context.h: Irish and EU rules affecting ships on the Shannon Estuary
p: Ireland is an EU member state and a Paris MoU member, and the Marine Survey Office of the Department of Transport is the body that inspects foreign ships under port state control. Bulk carriers and tankers in the estuary trades are ESP ships, so their renewal surveys and intermediate surveys call for measured thickness of tanks, holds and bulkheads at the intervals set by their class society. Older ships fixed for the Shannon trades are also likely to meet charterer scrutiny, and a clear set of recent readings helps a manager answer questions before they turn into delays.

Ships calling at EU ports must carry an Inventory of Hazardous Materials under the EU Ship Recycling Regulation, and the EU's emissions trading scheme and FuelEU Maritime both apply to voyages into Irish waters. For owners of older bulk tonnage on Irish trades, those rules make a long-term steel-condition record more valuable, because decisions on whether to renew steel, retrofit or recycle the ship rest on measured wastage rather than estimates. The estuary's industrial customers, which include a refinery and generating stations, also apply their own acceptance standards to ships using their jetties.

jobs.h: Typical gauging jobs on the Shannon Estuary
jobs.p: Work here follows the bulk trades. A job usually begins with the manager's survey programme, which we turn into a plan that matches the cargo and the berth. Because discharge is slow and pilotage is tide-dependent, there is normally time to agree the plan with the master before boarding. Readings are delivered in the format the class surveyor and the yard will use, and, where the ship will dock elsewhere, are timed so the steel estimate is ready before the yard slot is confirmed.
list: Hold and hopper tank gauging on a Supramax carrying feed or fertiliser, staged with the discharge so each hold is measured once clear.
Intermediate survey preparation on a bulk carrier at Foynes, covering topside and ballast tanks and the lower hold frames.
Pre-docking steel estimate for a coaster or product tanker, so the yard on another coast can plan renewals before arrival.
Deck and piping gauging on a fuel-supply tanker alongside a power-station jetty, within the terminal's permit rules.
Owner's condition gauging of a bulk carrier at anchor in the estuary before a sale or charter.

logistics: Shannon Airport is the nearest international airport, and Dublin and Cork are the usual alternatives for long-haul arrivals, followed by a road transfer. Technicians travel from India on Irish visas, which are separate from the Schengen visa and are applied for once the ship's schedule is known. Access to the Foynes quays and to the private jetties is arranged through the ship's agent, and anchorage launches are booked by the same route, with the plan allowing a margin for late arrivals and weather.
vessels: Coasters and short-sea general cargo ships

faqs.q: Can a bulk carrier be gauged while it is discharging at Foynes?
faqs.a: Yes. Discharge at Foynes takes several days, and tanks and deck areas away from the grabs can be gauged while it continues. Holds are entered once the stevedores have emptied and the crew have cleaned them. The plan is agreed with the master so that gauging and cargo work do not interfere, and readings are reported hold by hold.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock on the Shannon Estuary?
faqs.a: There is no drydock on the estuary. Ships that need a docking go to a yard on another coast, and the gauging done at Foynes or at anchor serves as the pre-docking survey. Having measured thickness in advance lets the yard scope steel renewal before the ship arrives, which shortens the docking.

faqs.q: Can you gauge tanks at the anchorage while a ship waits for a berth?
faqs.a: Yes, when the tanks are clean, gas-free and certified safe to enter, and the sea state allows a launch. Scattery Roads and the other estuary anchorages are sheltered compared with the open coast, but a westerly swell can stop launch work for a day. We plan with the agent and keep a reserve day where the schedule allows.

faqs.q: Do the refinery and power-station jetties allow outside contractors?
faqs.a: They do under their own rules. Each terminal expects a permit, an induction for named personnel and agreement from the master, and cargo operations can restrict the areas available. We submit names and the scope through the ship's agent in good time and keep the work to the areas released on the day.
